Explain what matters most in the purchase: the intended application, a confirmed product design, a target purchase date or compatibility with existing equipment. A clear brief is more useful than an unsupported target price. We review the project rather than treating a high budget as proof of a genuine buyer.

sections.heading: Keep Product Changes Visible During Quotation
paragraphs: A price based on one product revision should not silently become a price for another. If the design is still changing, list the open decisions and tell us when you expect to finalize them. Give revised files clear names and identify what has changed.

After the quotation, record any agreed scope change together with its possible cost and schedule effects. The same principle applies to a change in mold quantity, intended equipment or acceptance requirements. A written comparison trail helps your purchasing and engineering teams understand why two quotation versions differ.

h1: What to Prepare for a Die Casting Mold Quotation
intro: You do not need a finished mold design to ask about a custom mold. You do need a clear reference for the product the mold will make. For EXACTMEC, that means clear product 2D or 3D drawings, or a physical sample. This checklist explains what to prepare now, what can follow in conversation and how to avoid mixing product information with the mold design we prepare after payment.

sections.heading: Start With One Clear Product Reference
paragraphs: Clear 2D drawings, 3D drawings or an actual sample give us a basis for evaluating the mold request. If you have more than one type, tell us which information is current and whether the files describe the same product. Make the units and revision clear.

An image of a drawing may be difficult to interpret when dimensions or notes are blurred. Check readability before sending files during follow-up. If you only have a sample, explain whether it represents the exact product you want or a reference that needs changes. We can then discuss the next assessment steps.

Treat these as requests for assessment, not capabilities automatically confirmed by a website example. An approximate per-mold budget is optional. If you share it, include the currency and clarify whether it covers tooling alone. You can also say that the budget is undecided. description: Plan the buyer's decisions from product reference and quotation to 3D mold design approval, manufacturing, trial samples, customer testing and mold shipment.
h1: Die Casting Mold Development: What Buyers Need to Plan
intro: Buying a custom mold involves decisions as well as manufacturing. A product drawing, an approved mold design and an approved trial sample each answer a different question. This guide explains how to prepare your team for those decisions and avoid an unclear handover. It follows EXACTMEC's mold-only supply model: quotation from product drawings or a sample, design after payment, customer approval, manufacturing, trial samples and final mold shipment.

paragraphs: Begin with the product the mold needs to make. Clear product 2D or 3D drawings, or an actual sample, provide the starting basis for an EXACTMEC quotation. Explain whether the reference is final and identify any changes still being considered.

Ask your purchasing and technical teams to use the same revision. If a sample is the reference, state which details must be reproduced and which need discussion. A simple list of open points helps prevent an early estimate being mistaken for agreement on an unfinished specification. Submit basic project details first; the website form does not upload files.

sections.heading: 2. Turn the Quotation Into a Shared Project Scope
paragraphs: Before payment, ask what the quotation covers and what still requires agreement. Confirm mold quantity, design work, trial arrangements, sample expectations and the proposed delivery sequence. Payment terms, freight and change-related costs are discussed for the individual project.

Separate the tool purchase from the production of finished cast parts. EXACTMEC accepts one mold set and does not currently accept die casting mass-production orders. If your own production team or another supplier will run the finished mold, involve them early enough to provide the relevant equipment and acceptance information. Do not assume that sending a mold drawing to an unrelated team at the end will resolve every interface question.

sections.heading: 3. Make Time for 3D Mold Design Approval
paragraphs: After payment, we prepare the 3D mold design and send it to you for approval. Manufacturing begins only after you confirm that design. This is a separate stage from providing the product drawing used for quotation.

Decide who can approve the design and who needs to review it internally. Consolidate questions into a clear response rather than sending conflicting instructions from several contacts. If a point is unclear, ask for an explanation before approving it. Keep the approval record tied to an identifiable design version so purchasing, engineering and the project contact can refer to the same decision.

sections.heading: 4. Build a Schedule Around Decisions, Not One Date
paragraphs: The general production estimate is approximately 30–40 days from payment. Design approval follows payment and is part of the project sequence. Confirm the covered milestones and exact timing for your project; the estimate does not guarantee a door-to-door delivery date.

Plan internal review time, trial work, sample transport, customer testing and final mold transport as distinct milestones. Tell us if your company has a fixed launch or equipment-installation date. Ask how an unresolved design decision or a later product change would affect the agreed plan before relying on the estimate for downstream commitments.

sections.heading: 5. Prepare for Trial Samples Before They Arrive
paragraphs: After the mold is manufactured, we carry out a mold trial and send produced samples for your testing. Your team then checks the samples against the agreed requirements. This is a customer decision point before final mold shipment.

Prepare who will inspect the samples, what they will check and how the results will be recorded. Use the same agreed product reference. If you find a problem, provide specific observations and supporting information so the issue can be discussed. A later change to the product should be identified separately from feedback on whether a sample meets the existing requirement. Adjustment scope, cost and timing need project-specific agreement.

sections.heading: 6. Confirm Acceptance Before Final Mold Shipment
paragraphs: We arrange shipment of the finished mold after you test the samples and confirm there is no issue. Sample approval does not lead to a mass-production order with EXACTMEC; the next step in this supply model is the mold handover.

Before that handover, confirm the delivery destination, receiving contact and agreed shipping arrangements. Ask which project information accompanies the mold and resolve outstanding commercial details. Avoid assuming that a website process diagram settles packing costs, freight, import responsibilities or every document needed at the destination. Those details belong in the project agreement and shipping discussion.

sections.heading: 7. Keep a Short Decision Record Throughout the Project
paragraphs: A useful project record can be simple: current product revision, current mold design revision, open questions, approvals and next actions. Give each open question an owner. When your team changes a requirement, explain what changed instead of sending a new file without context.

This record supports continuity if purchasing, engineering or the receiving team joins at a different stage. It also helps distinguish confirmed scope from an idea discussed informally. Start your inquiry with the information already available, be clear about the gaps and use the follow-up conversation to resolve the next decision rather than attempting to settle everything in the first form.
